title: Learning to Be Monitored: Causal Bounds and Intervention-Aware Post-Training Recipes for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
content:
Computer Science > Machine Learning

Title:Learning to Be Monitored: Causal Bounds and Intervention-Aware Post-Training Recipes for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring aims to detect potentially harmful behaviors in large language models (LLMs) from their CoTs. Intervention-based evaluations measure this property by asking whether a monitor can detect the role of an intervention from the CoT when the targeted behavior occurs, typically using minimal-criterion sensitivity ($\mathsf{TPR_{mc}}$) proposed by~\citep{guan2025monitoring}. However, a target behavior observed under intervention is not necessarily caused by it, and we show that this metric can overestimate how often a monitor detects target behaviors actually caused by the intervention. Specifically, we establish $\mathsf{TPR_{mc}}$ as an upper bound on this causal detection rate and derive a complementary lower bound, which provides a tighter evaluation framework for CoT monitorability. With this framework, we study whether LLMs can be trained to make their CoTs easier to monitor. We first construct a training dataset of paired control--intervention tasks spanning multiple intervention types. Using the dataset, we design and apply three intervention-specific training methods based on off-policy self-distillation, reinforcement learning, and on-policy self-distillation to train separate variants of each base model. Across various model-monitor configurations, all three methods generally improve CoT monitorability over the corresponding base models under our extended evaluation framework. Our code is available at this https URL.

report.summary: New research tightens how we measure chain-of-thought monitorability and shows post-training can make LLM reasoning easier to monitor.
report.background: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring uses a model's written reasoning as a safety check: if the CoT reveals a harmful plan, a monitor can flag it. Prior intervention-based evaluations ask whether a monitor can detect when an intervention caused a target behavior, often using minimal-criterion sensitivity (TPR_mc). But the paper argues that observing a target behavior under intervention does not prove the intervention caused it, so TPR_mc can overestimate how often monitors detect causally induced behaviors. The authors frame TPR_mc as an upper bound and derive a complementary lower bound for a tighter evaluation. They then test whether models can be trained to produce more monitorable CoTs, using paired control-intervention tasks and three post-training methods. This matters because CoT monitoring is increasingly proposed as an oversight layer for high-stakes LLM deployment.
key_points: The paper identifies a measurement flaw: existing intervention-based CoT monitoring scores can count behaviors that appear during an intervention but were not actually caused by it, inflating apparent monitor success.

It establishes the common minimal-criterion sensitivity metric as an upper bound on causal detection and derives a lower bound, giving evaluators a tighter range for how well monitors detect intervention-caused behavior.

The authors build a training dataset of paired control and intervention tasks spanning multiple intervention types, enabling models to be trained specifically for monitorability rather than only task accuracy.

Three post-training recipes are tested: off-policy self-distillation, reinforcement learning, and on-policy self-distillation. Each produces model variants trained to make their CoTs easier for monitors to interpret.
Across several model-monitor configurations, all three methods generally improve CoT monitorability over base models under the extended causal evaluation framework, though gains vary by setup.
The work links evaluation methodology to training incentives: instead of only measuring whether CoTs are monitorable, it shows post-training can deliberately shape that property.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this paper raises the bar for safety claims based on CoT monitoring: stronger evaluations must separate correlation from causation when judging whether a monitor catches harmful reasoning. For developers, it offers a practical recipe for post-training models to be more monitorable, but also warns that monitorability is not automatic and may trade off with capability, helpfulness, or privacy of reasoning. For regular users, the upside is more reliable oversight of AI systems in high-stakes settings; the caveat is that better monitorability does not guarantee safety, because monitors can still fail and models may learn to appear compliant. The causal-bounds framework is likely most useful as an evaluation standard and as a design target for future post-training pipelines.
report.tools: The paper says code is available via its arXiv page, so start there for the exact implementation. For follow-up work, use Inspect (UK AISI) for structured model evaluations, TransformerLens for CoT and activation analysis, and lm-evaluation-harness or OpenAI Evals as benchmark harnesses. Watch the Guan et al. minimal-criterion sensitivity implementation and paired control-intervention datasets. These tools help replicate causal-bound evaluations and compare monitor configurations, but they do not replace the paper's intervention-aware methodology.
